title: Why a MILP has no duals

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A reporting script solves a crew-scheduling MILP to OPTIMAL with HiGHS through MathOpt, then calls result.dual_values() on its labour row. What happens, and what should the script have checked first?

options.text: It returns zero duals for every row; it should have checked the gap first
options.says: The page shows no zeros: the call raises, because the result carries no dual solution.

options.text: It raises ValueError; it should have checked has_dual_feasible_solution()
options.says: Right: the MILP's result has no dual feasible solution, and dual_values raises ValueError, so check the flag first.

options.text: It returns the relaxation's duals; it should have checked the model type first
options.says: MathOpt does not substitute the LP relaxation's prices; the call raises.

options.text: It returns the last node's prices; it should have checked the node count first
options.says: No node's prices are returned; the result has no dual solution at all.

origin.section: A Solver Reports No Dual Values for a MILP

questions.stem: A one-row integer program has z(6) = 9, z(7) = 9 and z(8) = 13. Which price per unit supports z at d = 7, so that z(d') <= z(7) + p (d' - 7) for every d'?

options.text: Price 4, since the next unit is worth 4 and a price looks forward
options.says: A price must also be at most the backward slope, which is 0 here, so 4 fails.

options.text: Price 0, since the last unit was worth 0 and a price looks back
options.says: A price must be at least the forward slope, 4, so 0 fails.

options.text: Price 2, since that is the average of the two neighbouring slopes
options.says: 2 is below the forward slope of 4, so the line passes under z(8).

options.text: No price, since the next unit is worth 4 and the last worth 0
options.says: Right: p >= 4 and p <= 0 cannot both hold, so no line touches z from above at 7.

origin.section: A Price Is a Line That Touches the Value Function From Above, and a Step Function Has Almost None

questions.stem: For a one-row maximization in whole numbers, a planner offers F(d) = 3 floor(d/2). It has F(0) = 0, F(1) >= 0, is superadditive, and meets F(a_j) >= c_j for every column. What does F(11) = 15 tell you?

options.text: No plan using 11 units is worth more than 15
options.says: Right: a dual-feasible F bounds every plan's value at its right side (weak duality).

options.text: Some plan using 11 units is worth exactly 15
options.says: Weak duality gives a bound, not a plan; only the value function is sure to be attained.

options.text: The unit after 11 is worth 3 to the best plan
options.says: F is a bound on values, not a forecast of the next unit's worth.

options.text: Every plan using 11 units is worth at least 15
options.says: The bound runs the other way: every plan is worth at most F(11).

origin.section: A MILP's Dual Is a Function, Not a Number
